newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan opposition party ignores recent defections.
newsitem.headline: Japan opposition party ignores recent defections.

text.p: Japan's main opposition party on Wednesday turned a blind eye to the squabble that has led to the defection of nearly one-fifth of its members.
Shinshinto (New Frontier) Party legislators gathered in Tokyo to debate the party's new platform, one day after five party members quit the party.
But party leader Ichiro Ozawa failed to mention the defections in his opening speech.
A word of reprimand against the five came only from Takeo Nishioka, the party's secretary-general.

"We have avoided openly criticising those who once gathered under the common goal for reform...but a move to support forces which fail to conduct comprehensive reform is an act of benefiting the enemy," Nishioka said.

The five who submitted resignations cited policy differences with Ozawa and bring to 32 the number of legislators who have quit the party since it won 156 seats in lower house election in October 1996.
The move follows signs of the party declining as a political force.
Earlier this month, Shinshinto suffered a major blow when it failed to win any seat in the Tokyo local government elections.
And only hours after the elections results, a key Ozawa aide, former defence minister Kazuo Aichi, quit the party over "policy differences" with his autocratic leader.
Ozawa shrugged off suggestions that he should resign to take responsibility for his party's crumbling strength, saying he was "not interested in the numbers game".
Political analysts say more defections could follow because resentment towards Ozawa is strong among some party members.

Those opposing Ozawa criticise his refusal to step down after the poor election showing, as well as his high-handed management style and moves to form a conservative coalition with the ruling Liberal Democratic Party.
A poll released on Wednesday showed public support for Shinshinto plunging to 6.8 percent, its lowest since the party's launch in December 1994.
The next national-level elections are due in July 1998 for half of the 252 seats in parliament's Upper House, a less influential chamber than the Lower House.
